background.text: And you're a millionaire now, as is well documented—in 13 years. Not a bad effort. How did you do it?

ground_truth: I think a hell of a lot is to do with the fact that I'm an immigrant, a child of an immigrant family. And there's a sort of dissatisfaction. Dissatisfaction creates an enormous amount of energy. And whenever I'm dissatisfied about anything, I push that into some sort of practical way of doing things. And so you wear that very comfortably—and hey presto, that's how you do it.

background.speaker: Interviewer
background.text: When you received the Company of the Year award, you were quite scathing about big business. What have you got against big business as it operates today?

ground_truth: I find business—in any profession—is probably the most conservative, pedantic, and boring. They're run by men, usually about 65-plus, who have no belief at all that they should be the agents of social change. Okay, so you come into... flew down into a major city—no, that's the wrong example. Let's say a major capital city 500 years ago. What would draw you into the city? The church spires or the church steeples—they gave the city a sense of purpose. You go into the city now, and you have huge edifices to money and to business. And there is no sense of purpose with that. And we see what's happening in the government, where the government is pulling back education, social services. Businesses have got to push forward. They've got to be much more linked with the community. They've got to fly the flag of social change. So I basically said... you're fearful. You know, do you try and talk about the word 'love'? You bring up the word 'love' in business—it's as fearful as any other four-letter word. You can't talk about it. It's too feminine for them.
